title: Leadership Why Contemplating Your Death Might Make You Happier Arthur Brooks
author: Brooks, Arthur
summary: Drawing on the experience of watching his father approach death with peace and on psychological research, Brooks argues that deliberately contemplating mortality improves both happiness and decision-making. Research shows people involuntarily dissociate their own face from death-related words — a built-in drive to avoid the association — yet mortality salience can paradoxically encourage positive thinking (2007 research). Brooks offers three practical exercises: making daily death contemplation a routine ('I know that in a few years I will be dead. But I am alive today, and I will not waste it'), surveying life goals to identify what truly matters by imagining a terminal diagnosis, and thinking about the good one's efforts will produce for future generations — not as legacy-building but as present-moment meaning. Contemplating death is not grim; it is clarifying.
points: Most people involuntarily avoid associating death with themselves — an experimental finding, not an observation — yet this avoidance comes at a cost to priorities and decisions.
Mortality salience can encourage positive thinking: it helps people choose constructive framings of the present moment rather than defaulting to distraction.
Practical exercise: count the remaining Thanksgivings you will share with your parents — a concrete number that alters life decisions more powerfully than abstract reflection.
Daily death contemplation routine: 'I know that in a few years I will be dead. But I am alive today, and I will not waste it' — brings energy and intentionality to the day.
Thinking about good that outlasts you — enriching future generations regardless of whether they know your name — provides present-moment meaning without requiring belief in legacy.
quotes: Near the end of his life when he was very sick but had accepted what was coming, he reflected quite a bit on his passing. It wasn't sad or grim, though. On the contrary, it seemed to give him a sense of peace and perspective.

But by forcing ourselves to think about death — our own death and that of loved ones — our resource-use decisions change. Rarely, if ever, have I heard anyone regret deciding to live near friends and family — any more than I recall hearing someone say, as they near death, 'I sure wish I'd spent more time on United Airlines.'

Paradoxical though it may seem, doing so can encourage positive thinking, as researchers found in 2007. It encourages you to think extremely clearly, and realize that you have a choice about how to see the present moment — and choose the more positive alternative.

For the sake of some future reward, are you neglecting your family life today? Your friendships? Your spiritual development? Envision yourself having just months to live and giving your current self some life advice. You're probably not saying, 'The health of your marriage can wait; use all your time now to make it to assistant regional manager for sales!'

Whether you are religious or not, some psychologists posit that this is a good way to experience deeper meaning in the here and now. I don't mean that you should struggle to achieve some glorious legacy. Rather, the idea is to think of how your efforts to make life better for others will enrich future generations, regardless of whether they know your name.
